paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Practice 49: The Piano Upstairs (§B style, standard band)
provenanceNote: NOT STUDENT-FACING. Original narrative written for the morning-quiz bank; NOT from any past exam paper. Section B [19 marks], 1184/02 §B format, SEAB assessment objectives. 10 short-answer items (mixed [1]/[2]) + 4-blank emotion flowchart split for independent auto-grading.

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below about a woman who complains for two years about the piano in the flat above her, and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
For twenty-two months the piano started at seven and stopped at eight. The same four bars, over and over, always breaking at the same place, as though the player reached a wall there and had to walk back to the beginning to try again.

Paragraph 2
I work night shifts. Seven in the evening is my four in the morning. I wrote three letters. The first was reasonable. The second was less so. The third I did not send, which is the only decision from that period I am still content with.

Paragraph 3
I complained to the management office twice. A young man there told me, with the flat patience of someone who has said it many times, that music before ten at night is within the rules, and that he was sorry.

Paragraph 4
I began to hate the four bars in a way I could not have explained to anyone. I knew where the mistake would come. I would lie there waiting for it, and it would come, and something in me would tighten.

Paragraph 5
In October it stopped. I noticed on the fourth evening — not the first, which tells you something about how little we notice peace. For a week I slept properly. In the second week the silence began to sit oddly in the room, and I found myself, at ten past seven, listening.

Paragraph 6
I met the mother at the lift in November. I had rehearsed a cool nod. Instead she said, before I could arrange my face, that she hoped her daughter had not disturbed me, and that we would not be troubled any more, because the girl had passed her Grade Eight examination in September and had gone up to her aunt's place in Ipoh for a while.

Paragraph 7
I said something about it being no trouble, which was a lie of the ordinary kind.

Paragraph 8
Then she said: 'She practised that one piece for two years. She could not get the middle part. She said she would not move on until it was right.'

Paragraph 9
I thought about that all the way up in the lift. Twenty-two months of a child refusing to skip a difficult passage. I had lain one floor below listening to the most stubborn act of discipline I had ever encountered, and I had heard only noise.

Paragraph 10
The flat above me is quiet now. Somebody new moved in at the end of the year; they play the television loudly and I do not mind it at all. What I miss, on certain evenings, is being reminded that somewhere above my ceiling a person was refusing to give up on four bars of music.

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, describe TWO things that were always the same about the playing. [1]
questions.answer: it was the same four bars, and it always broke down at the same point

questions.stem: Q2. Using your own words, explain why the seven o'clock playing affected the narrator so severely. (Paragraph 2) [2]
questions.answer: ① she works nights, so early evening is the middle of her sleeping hours; ② the noise therefore struck her when she was least able to tolerate it, at a time everyone else considers reasonable

questions.stem: Q3. Why is the narrator 'still content with' her decision not to send the third letter? (Paragraph 2) [1]
questions.answer: it was written in anger and would have been unfair to the family

questions.stem: Q4. What is the effect of the image of the player reaching 'a wall' in Paragraph 1? [2]
questions.answer: it conveys the sense of an obstacle the player cannot pass, and the repeated return to the beginning makes the practice feel both endless and futile to a listener who does not know what it is for

questions.stem: Q5. From Paragraph 3, what reason did the management office give for not acting? [1]
questions.answer: playing music before ten at night did not break any rule

questions.stem: Q6. What is the effect of the narrator lying in wait for the mistake she knew was coming? (Paragraph 4) [2]
questions.answer: it shows the irritation had become an obsession she fed herself — anticipating the error made it worse than the sound itself, so most of her suffering was of her own making

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain what the narrator means by 'how little we notice peace'. (Paragraph 5) [2]
questions.answer: ① she took four days to register that the noise had ended; ② people register what disturbs them but let quiet pass unremarked, so relief goes unappreciated in a way annoyance never does

questions.stem: Q8. What does the narrator's behaviour at 'ten past seven' in the second week suggest? (Paragraph 5) [1]
questions.answer: she had grown used to the playing and was unconsciously waiting for it / missing it

questions.stem: Q9. Using your own words, explain why the mother's explanation in Paragraph 8 changed the narrator's view. [2]
questions.answer: ① what she had heard as incompetent noise was in fact a child refusing to skip a passage she could not yet play; ② the repetition she resented was evidence of unusual discipline rather than carelessness

questions.stem: Q10. What is the effect of the contrast in the final paragraph between the loud television and the piano? [1]
questions.answer: the louder noise does not trouble her at all, showing that what she resented was never really the volume but her own misreading of it

sections.instruction: Q11. [4 marks in total] The narrator's dominant feeling changes over the twenty-two months and after. For each part of the passage below, choose the ONE word from the bank that best describes how she feels at that moment. Each word may be used once only.
sections.passage: Refer to the same 'The Piano Upstairs' narrative in Exercise 1 above. Read the paragraphs named in each question, then choose the single word from the bank that best describes how the narrator feels at that moment.
